units.text: RATIONALITY OF THE MULTIVARIATE GROWTH SERIES FOR ALGEBRAIC SETS OF VIRTUALLY ABELIAN GROUPS
Introduction

Let G be a group, S ⊂ G be a finite subset, and ω : S → Z >0 be a positive integer weight.Let S * be the set of all words from S. For a word σ = s 1 • • • s ℓ ∈ S * , we define ω(σ) := ℓ i=1 ω(s i ).For g ∈ G, we define ω(g) as the smallest ω(σ) for all words σ that represent g.The growth series S G,S,ω (t) of G with respect to S and ω is defined as a formal power series
S G,S,ω (t) := i≥0 f G,S,ω (i)t i ∈ Z[[t]],
where f G,S,ω (i) := #{g ∈ G | ω(g) = i}.In [Ben83], Benson proved that the growth series S G,S,ω (t) is a rational function when G is a virtually abelian group.

An n-dimensional periodic graph (Γ, L) is a pair of a directed graph Γ (that may have loops and multiple edges) and a free abelian group L of rank n such that L freely acts on Γ and its quotient graph Γ/L is finite (see Definition 2.2).For a vertex x 0 of Γ, the growth series S Γ,x 0 (t) of Γ with respect to x 0 is defined by
S Γ,x 0 (t) := i≥0 f Γ,x 0 (i)t i ∈ Z[[t]],

where f Γ,x 0 (i) is defined as the number of vertices of Γ whose distance from x 0 is i.The sequence (f Γ,x 0 (i)) i is studied in both areas of crystallography and combinatorics (cf.[GSS19,Introduction]).Furthermore, this is also studied in relation to the Ehrhart theory (cf.[IN24,IN]).

In [GKBS96], Grosse-Kunstleve, Brunner and Sloane conjectured that the growth series S Γ,x 0 (t) of periodic graphs Γ are always rational functions.In [NSMN21], the author, Sakamoto, Mase and Nakagawa proved that this conjecture is true (see Theorem 2.3).This result is a generalization of Benson's theorem since the Cayley graphs of virtually abelian groups are periodic graphs (see Remark 2.7).In the proof of Theorem 2.3, they use the commutative monoid theory, and the proof is essentially different from Benson's original proof of Theorem 2.6, where he uses his theory of "polyhedral sets".

The rationality of the growth series S G,S,ω (t) is also proved for hyperbolic groups in [Can84,Gro87] and for the integer Heisenberg group in [DS19].Furthermore, some variants of growth series, such as the conjugacy growth series and the relative growth series, have been studied for many groups (cf.[GS10, DO15, AC17, CHHR16, Eve19]).

In [EL22], Evetts and Levine generalize Benson's theorem to the univariate relative growth series for algebraic sets of virtually abelian groups.For a positive integer d, a subset U ⊂ G d is called algebraic if U is the set of solutions of a finite system of equations with d variables whose coefficients are in G (see Definition 4.1).The univariate (relative) growth series S uni U,S,ω (t) of U with respect to S and ω is defined by
S uni U,S,ω (t) := x∈U t ω(x) ∈ Z[[t]],
where ω(x) := ℓ i=1 ω(x i ).Furthermore, the multivariate (relative) growth series S U,S,ω (z) is defined by
S U,S,ω (z) := x∈U z ω(x 1 ) 1 z ω(x 2 ) 2 • • • z ω(x d ) d ∈ Z[[z 1 , . . . , z d ]].

In [EL22], for any algebraic sets of any virtually abelian groups, the univariate growth series are proved to be rational functions ([EL22, Theorem 4.3]), and furthermore, the multivariate growth series are proved to be holonomic functions ([EL22, Corollary 4.21]).However, the rationality of the multivariate growth series remained a conjecture ([EL22, Conjecture 5.1]).The purpose of this paper is to give an affirmative answer to this conjecture.

Theorem 1.1 (= Theorem 4.4).Let G be a finitely generated virtually abelian group, S ⊂ G a finite subset, and ω a positive integer weight.Then, for any algebraic subset U ⊂ G d of G, its multivariate growth series S Y,S,ω (z) is a rational function.
Theorem 1.1 is a consequence of Theorem 3.5, which is the corresponding theorem for periodic graphs.The idea of the proof of Theorem 3.5 is to use an algebraic structure on the graded growth set

which is studied in [NSMN21] (see Appendix A).In [IN], further structure of B, which is not used in this paper, is studied as an analogy to the Ehrhart ring.We believe that these ideas have potential for further applications to similar studies of virtually abelian groups.

The paper is organized as follows.In Section 2, we introduce some notations on graphs and groups, and we also summarize facts on commutative monoid theory which will be used in Section 3. In Section 3, we prove Theorem 3.5.In Section 4, we prove Theorem 4.4.In Appendix A, we explain the algebraic structure of the graded growth set B proved in [NSMN21].The proofs in Appendix A are essentially the same as those in [NSMN21], but streamlined for mathematicians.

Preliminaries
Notation 2.1.
• For a set X, #X denotes its cardinality, and 2 X denotes its power set.

2.1.Growth series of periodic graphs.In this paper, a graph means a directed weighted graph which may have loops and multiple edges.More precisely, a graph Γ = (V Γ , E Γ , s Γ , t Γ , w Γ ) consists of the set V Γ of vertices, the set E Γ of edges, the source function s Γ : E Γ → V Γ , the target function t Γ : E Γ → V Γ , and the weight function w Γ : E Γ → Z >0 .We abbreviate s Γ , t Γ and w Γ to s, t and w when no confusion can arise.

Let Γ be a graph.A walk p is a sequence e 1 e 2 • • • e ℓ of edges e i ∈ V Γ satisfying t(e i ) = s(e i+1 ) for all 1 ≤ i ≤ ℓ − 1.We define the weight w(p) of p by w(p) := ℓ i=1 w(e i ).For x, y ∈ V Γ , we define d Γ (x, y) ∈ Z ≥0 ∪ {∞} as the smallest weight w(p) of any walk p = e 1 e 2 • • • e ℓ with x = s(e 1 ) and y = t(e ℓ ).Then, for
x 0 ∈ V Γ and i ∈ Z ≥0 , f Γ,x 0 (i) ∈ Z ≥0 is defined as f Γ,x 0 (i) := #{y ∈ V Γ | d Γ (x 0 , y) = i}.
The sequence (f Γ,x 0 (i)) i is called the growth sequence of Γ with respect to x 0 .The growth series S Γ,x 0 (t) of Γ with respect to x 0 is defined as its generating function
S Γ,x 0 (t) := i≥0 f Γ,x 0 (i)t i .
Definition 2.2 (cf.[IN24]).
(1) Let Γ be a graph, and let G be a group.A G-action on Γ means G-actions on V Γ and E Γ which preserve the edge relations and the weight function, i.e., for any u ∈ G and e ∈ E Γ , we have
s Γ (u(e)) = u(s Γ (e)), t Γ (u(e)) = u(t Γ (e)), w Γ (u(e)) = w Γ (e).
(2) Let n be a positive integer.An n-dimensional periodic graph (Γ, L) is a free abelian group L ≃ Z n of rank n and a graph Γ with an L-action satisfying the following two conditions:
• The L-actions on V Γ and E Γ are free, i.e., no non-trivial element of G fixes an element of V Γ and E Γ .• Their quotient sets V Γ /L and E Γ /L are finite sets.
The growth series of periodic graphs are known to be rational functions.

Theorem 2.3 ([NSMN21, Theorem 2.2]).Let (Γ, L) be a periodic graph, and let x 0 ∈ V Γ .Then, its growth sequence (f Γ,x 0 (i)) i is quasi-polynomial type.In particular, its growth series S Γ,x 0 (t) is a rational function.
Growth series of groups.
Let G be a group, S ⊂ G a finite subset, and ω : S → Z >0 a positive integer weight.Let S * be the set of all words from S. For a word
σ = s 1 • • • s ℓ ∈ S * , we define ω(σ) := ℓ i=1 ω(s i ).
For g ∈ G, we define ω(g) as the smallest ω(σ) for all words σ that represent g.By convention, we define ω(g) = ∞ if g cannot be represented by S.Then, for i ∈ Z ≥0 , f G,S,ω (i) ∈ Z ≥0 is defined as
f G,S,ω (i) := #{g ∈ G | ω(g) = i}.
The sequence (f G,S,ω (i)) i is called the growth sequence of G with respect to S and ω.The growth series S Γ,S,ω (t) of G with respect to S and ω is its generating function
S G,S,ω (t) := i≥0 f G,S,ω (i)t i .
Remark 2.4.We need not to assume that S generates G even in Theorems 2.6 and 4.4.
Remark 2.5.The (right) Cayley graph Γ = Γ G,S,ω of G with respect to S and ω is defined as follows:
• V Γ := G. • E Γ := G × S. • For e = (g, s) ∈ E Γ , we define s Γ (e) = g, t Γ (e) = gs, w Γ (e) = ω(s).
Then, the number f G,S,ω (i) defined above coincides with the growth sequence f Γ,1 G (i) of the graph Γ defined in Section 2.1.

A group G is called virtually abelian if there exists an abelian subgroup H of G with finite index [G : H] < ∞.In [Ben83], Benson proved that the growth series of virtually abelian groups are rational functions.

Theorem 2.6 (Benson [Ben83]).Let G be a finitely generated virtually abelian group, S ⊂ G a finite subset, and ω a positive integer weight.Then, the sequence (f G,S,ω (i)) i is of quasi-polynomial type.In particular, its growth series S G,S,ω (t) is a rational function.

Remark 2.7.When G is a finitely generated virtually abelian group, we may take a free abelian subgroup L < G of finite rank and of finite index.Since L is a subgroup of G, the left L-action on G induces a free L-action on the Cayley graph Γ = Γ G,S,ω .Furthermore, since L is a subgroup of G with finite index, the quotient graph Γ/L is a finite graph.Therefore, the Cayley graph Γ is a periodic graph.Hence, Theorem 2.6 can be seen as a special case of Theorem 2.3.

Benson's original proof of Theorem 2.6 uses his theory of "polyhedral sets".On the other hand, the proof of Theorem 2.3 uses the theory of commutative monoid explained in Subsection 2.3, and the argument is quite different from Benson's argument.

2.3.Some facts in commutative monoid theory.The key tool of this paper is the rationality of the Hilbert series of finitely generated modules (Theorem 2.9).This is an important theorem in the context of algebraic geometry and commutative algebra, but it is also useful in enumerative combinatorics.

A commutative monoid M is called integral if it has the cancellation property (i.e., for any a, b, c ∈ M , a + b = a + c implies b = c).For a commutative monoid M , an Mmodule just means a set with an M -action.An M -module X is called finitely generated if X = x∈X ′ (M + x) holds for some finite subset X ′ ⊂ X.An M -module X is called a free M -module if there exists a subset X ′ ⊂ X such that any x ∈ X can be uniquely expressed as x = a + y with a ∈ M and y ∈ X ′ .For more detail on commutative monoid and its module theory, refer to [BG09] and [NSMN21].

Theorem 2.8(1) below is well-known in the theory of commutative monoid (cf.[Ogu18, Ch.I, Theorem 2.1.17.6], [BG09, Corollary 2.11]).Theorem 2.8(2) is proved in [NSMN21, Theorem A12].We note that Theorem 2.8(2) can be seen as a discrete version of Motzkin's theorem ([BG09, Theorem 1.27]).

Theorem 2.8.Let M be an integral commutative monoid, and let X be a free M -module.Let N 1 and N 2 be finitely generated submonoids of M .Let Y i ⊂ X be a finitely generated N i -submodule for i = 1, 2. Then the following assertions hold:
(1) N 1 ∩ N 2 is a finitely generated monoid.
(2) Y 1 ∩ Y 2 is a finitely generated (N 1 ∩ N 2 )-module.
The following theorem due to Hilbert and Serre is well-known in the theory of commutative algebra.The series H Y is called the Hilbert series.

Theorem 2.9 (cf.[BG09, Theorem 6.37]).Let d be a positive integer.Let M be a commutative monoid, and let X be an M -module.Let N ′ ⊂ Z d >0 ×M be a finite subset, and let N ⊂ Z d ≥0 × M be the submonoid generated by N ′ .Let Y ⊂ Z d ≥0 × X be a finitely generated N -submodule.We define a function h Y by
h Y : Z d ≥0 → Z ≥0 ; a → #{x ∈ X | (a, x) ∈ Y } Then, the series H Y (t) := a∈Z d ≥0 h Y (a)t a ∈ Z[[t 1 , . . . , t d ]]
is a rational function.Here, t a denotes t a 1 1 • • • t a d d for a = (a 1 , . . ., a d ).

Here, z a denotes z a 1 1 • • • z a d d for a = (a 1 , . . ., a d ).Theorem 3.5.Let d be a positive integer.Let N be a finitely generated submonoid of L d .Let Y be a finitely generated N -submodule of V d Γ .Then the multivariate growth series B Y,x 0 (z) and S Y,x 0 (z) of Y are rational functions.

Y,x 0 (z) = (1 − z 1 ) • • • (1 − z d )B Y,x 0 (z), it is sufficient to show that B Y,x 0 (z) is a rational function. For each a ∈ Z d ≥0 , we have B Y,a = B Y ∩ {a} × V d Γ . Since we have B = S∈2 V Γ /L X S by Theorem 3.1(1), we have B Y = S∈(2 V Γ /L ) d X Y,S .
By the inclusion-exclusion principle, in order to show the rationality of
B Y,x 0 (z) = a∈Z d ≥0 # S∈(2 V Γ /L ) d X Y,S ∩ {a} × V d Γ z a ,
it is sufficient to show the rationality of the series
H Λ (z) := a∈Z d ≥0 # S∈Λ X Y,S ∩ {a} × V d Γ z a
for each subset Λ ⊂ 2 V Γ /L d .By Theorem 2.9, the rationality of each H Λ (z) follows from Lemma 3.3.□
Rationality of the multivariate growth series of algebraic sets of virtually abelian groups
Following [EL22], we introduce a concept called "algebraic sets" for groups.
Definition 4.1.Let G be a group, and let d be a positive integer.
(1) A finite system of equations in G is a finite subset of G * F d , where F d is the free group generated by {X 1 , . . ., X d }.
(2) For w ∈ G * F d and (g 1 , . . ., g d ) ∈ G d , we define w(g 1 , . . ., g d ) ∈ G as follows: Let
f 1 : F d → G be the group homomorphism satisfying f 1 (X i ) = g i for each 1 ≤ i ≤ d.
Let f 2 : G * F d → G be the group homomorphism obtained by extending both f 1 and the identity map G → G.Then, we define w(g 1 , . . ., g d ) := f 2 (w) ∈ G.

(3) For a finite system W of equations in G, (g 1 , . . ., g d ) ∈ G d is called a solution of W when w(g 1 , . . ., g d ) = 1 G holds for all w ∈ W . (4) A subset U ⊂ G d is called algebraic if there exists a finite system W of equations in G such that U is the set of solutions of W .
Definition 4.2.Let G be a group, S ⊂ G be a finite subset, and ω be a positive integer weight.Let d be a positive integer, and let U ⊂ G d be a subset.
(1) We define multivariate (relative) growth series S U,S,ω (z) of U by
S U,S,ω (z) := x∈U z ω(x 1 ) 1 z ω(x 2 ) 2 • • • z ω(x d ) d ∈ Z[[z 1 , . . . , z d ]].

A.1.Notations and Preliminaries.Following [IN24, Section 2], we introduce some additional notations on graphs.
Definition A.1.Let Γ = (V Γ , E Γ , s, t, w) be a graph.
(1) For a walk p = e 1 e 2 • • • e ℓ , we define s(p) := s(e 1 ), t(p) := t(e ℓ ), length(p) = ℓ and supp(p) := {s(e 1 ), t(e 1 ), t(e 2 ), . . ., t(e ℓ )} ⊂ V Γ .

(2) A path in Γ is a walk e 1 e 2 • • • e ℓ such that s(e 1 ), t(e 1 ), t(e 2 ), . . ., t(e ℓ ) are distinct.A walk of length 0 is considered as a path.(3) A cycle in Γ is a walk e 1 e 2 • • • e ℓ with s(e 1 ) = t(e ℓ ) such that t(e 1 ), t(e 2 ), . . ., t(e ℓ ) are distinct.A walk of length 0 is not considered as a cycle.Cyc Γ denotes the set of cycles in Γ. (4) C 1 (Γ, Z) denotes the group of 1-chains on Γ with coefficients in Z (i.e., C 1 (Γ, Z)

is the free abelian group generated by E Γ ).For a walk p = e 1 e 2 • • • e ℓ in Γ, let ⟨p⟩ denote the 1-chain ℓ i=1 e i ∈ C 1 (Γ, Z).H 1 (Γ, Z) ⊂ C 1 (Γ, Z) denotes the 1st homology group (i.e., H 1 (Γ, Z) is the subgroup generated by ⟨p⟩ for p ∈ Cyc Γ ).We refer the reader to [Sun13] for more detail.
Definition A.2. Let (Γ, L) be an n-dimensional periodic graph.
(1) Since L is an abelian group, we use the additive notation defined by: for u ∈ L and x ∈ V Γ , we define u + x := u(x) as the translation of x by u.

(2) The quotient graph Γ/L = (V Γ/L , E Γ/L , s Γ/L , t Γ/L , w Γ/L ) is defined by V Γ/L := V Γ /L, E Γ/L := E Γ /L, and the functions s Γ/L : E Γ /L → V Γ /L, t Γ/L : E Γ /L → V Γ /L, and w Γ/L : E Γ /L → Z >0 induced from s Γ , t Γ , and w Γ . (3) For any x ∈ V Γ and e ∈ E Γ , let x ∈ V Γ/L and e ∈ E Γ/L denote their images in V Γ/L = V Γ /L and E Γ/L = E Γ /L. For a walk p = e 1 • • • e ℓ in Γ, let p := e 1 • • • e ℓ denote its image in Γ/L. (4

Lemma A.3 ([IN24, Lemma 2.12, Remark 2.13(2)]).Let (Γ, L) be an n-dimensional periodic graph.
(1) For a walk q ′ in Γ/L, there exists a walkable sequence (q 0 , q 1 , . . ., q ℓ ) such that ⟨q ′ ⟩ = ℓ i=0 ⟨q i ⟩ and supp(q ′ ) = ℓ i=0 supp(q i ).

(2) Let q 0 be a path in Γ/L, and let q 1 , . . ., q ℓ ∈ Cyc Γ/L be cycles.Then, (q 0 , q 1 , . . ., q ℓ ) is walkable if and only if there exists a permutation σ : {1, 2, . . ., ℓ} → {1, 2, . . ., ℓ} such that supp(q 0 ) ∪ 1≤i≤k supp(q σ(i) ) ∩ supp(q σ(k+1) ) ̸ = ∅ holds for any 0 ≤ k ≤ ℓ − 1.
